content.text: Speed and velocity both describe how fast an object is moving, but they are different quantities. Understanding this difference is crucial in physics, especially when analysing motion in different directions.
Speed tells you how fast something moves. Velocity tells you how fast AND in which direction. Speed is a scalar; velocity is a vector.

content.text: Average speed uses total distance and total time, while instantaneous speed is the speed at a particular moment. A car's speedometer shows instantaneous speed, while dividing journey distance by journey time gives average speed.

Spacecraft velocities are crucial for orbital mechanics - both speed AND direction determine the orbit.

Students often confuse speed and velocity in exam answers. If a question asks for velocity, you must state a direction (e.g. '15 m/s to the right'). If it asks for speed, just the magnitude is needed (e.g. '15 m/s').
— Speed is scalar (magnitude only); velocity is vector (magnitude and direction).
"An object moving at constant speed has constant velocity"
— Not if it changes direction! A car going around a bend at steady speed has changing velocity.
— An object can have high speed but zero average velocity (like running in circles).
— Negative velocity simply means moving in the negative direction (e.g., leftward when rightward is positive).
— Instantaneously, yes. But average velocity can be zero even if the object moved (if it returned to start).
